newsitem.title: UK: British opposition parties agree talks, deny pact.
newsitem.headline: British opposition parties agree talks, deny pact.

text.p: Britain's two main opposition parties on Tuesday announced a drive to coordinate policies on constitutional issues but denied the move was the prelude to a pact designed to oust the ruling Conservatives.

Despite predictions that it could have a large overall majority in parliament after an election due by May, the Labour Party said it would hold frequent pre-election meetings with the minority Liberal Democrats.

The two sides will seek agreement on how to set up separate parliaments for Scotland and Wales, reform the upper House of Lords, introduce a Bill of Rights and a Freedom of Information Act, and hold a referendum on changing the voting system.
"This is not a pact," Robin Cook, chairman of Labour's National Policy Forum, told a news conference.
"The Labour Party and the Liberal Democrats will fight the next election as distinct parties with separate candidates in every constituency, and there are broad areas of disagreement between us."
Liberal Democrat President Robert Maclennan also denied the talks were "linked to any hidden agenda".
He said they were designed to ensure changes to which both parties were committed to rid Britain of its outdated constitutional arrangements.
"Constitutional reform has in the past proved difficult to secure even for a government with a large majority," he said.

Cooperation in government between British political parties is rare, with the last instance being in 1977-8 when the Liberals concluded a pact with a Labour government which had lost its overall majority in parliament.

But the annual conference of the Liberal Democrats in September was dominated by the question of whether party leader Paddy Ashdown should accept approaches from Labour's Tony Blair if he becomes prime minister.

Some Liberals said Ashdown should accept a cabinet post if it was offered, while others warned that the Liberals, who at present have just 26 of the 651 seats in the House of Commons, would suffer electorally from any flirtation with Labour.

The Liberal Democrats are bound to press for proportional representation as the price of any cooperation -- at the 1992 election, the party won more than 17 percent of the votes but less than four percent of the seats.

Labour, which is committed to setting up a Scottish parliament within a year of taking office, had a lead of around 20 points over the Conservatives in most recent opinion polls, but there have been signs this lead is slipping.

Cook and Maclennan have been talking for months on constitutional matters. But Tuesday's announcement means that heavyweight teams from the two parties will now get together with party experts on constitutional matters.
